newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan's Lee says he not worried by Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan's Lee says he not worried by Deng's death.

text.p: Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui has urged people not to worry about the death of Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, saying the island faced worse threats during a recent missile crisis, local media said on Friday.
"We should not take this issue too seriously," Lee was quoted as telling a group of national assemblymen on Thursday.

"We have experienced the most dangerous missile crisis, so we should have confidence and not become unravelled," the Central Daily News newspaper, owned by the ruling Nationalist Party, quoted Lee as saying.
Nineteen months ago, China clamped a freeze on what had been slowly warming unofficial ties with Taiwan after a controversial visit to the United States by Lee in June 1995.

Beijing, which interpreted Lee's private but high-profile trip as an attempt to promote independence for Nationalist-held Taiwan, later staged several missile tests near the island to warn the Taiwanese not to drop a pledge for reunification.
The war games hit the island's financial markets in early 1996 and triggered panic buying of U.S. dollars and gold.

China has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949. Both governments say they want reunification but under very different terms, and Beijing refuses to drop its threat to use military force to retake the island should it declare independence.
State-run Central News Agency quoted Lee as saying on Friday that Taipei and Beijing were unlikely to resume semi-official talks before Beijing holds the 15th Communist Party congress in October.
The president said communist Chinese leadership would be occupied by political transition and would not have time for negotiation with Taiwan.

Lee, who said his government would continue to promote ties between the two rivals, predicted Taiwan-China talks would be reopened after China's President Jiang Zemin consolidated his power during the party congress.

Taiwan officials had asked people to remain calm after Deng's death in Beijing late on Wednesday. The island's sensitive stock market has so far shrugged off political fears, rising 0.28 percent on Thursday and a further 1.47 percent on Friday.
"It (Deng's death) happened and the stock market rose... We should set our heart at ease," Lee told the assemblymen.
"Nothing will be affected by them (China) and we have been prepared since a long time ago," the independent China Times newspaper quoted Lee as saying.
"Why should you worry if I am not worried?" Lee said.
